title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: ...government is also, I would say, a risk free business in a way. But the challenge is collecting at time.
epigraph.author: Vijay Gupta, Founder, Chairman and CEO, SoftTech Engineers, Q4 FY26 earnings call, 2 June 2026

web_blocks.html: SoftTech does not sell the way a consumer software firm does. There is no app store, no free trial and no sales army. It sells by tender. A housing department or port authority publishes a request for proposal (RFP), bidders submit technical and price bids, and an evaluation committee decides. The CEO describes the discipline this way: 'we get engaged with the customer before RFP is published', explaining the value, and the company works 'on specific opportunities only rather than going with all different types of RFPs' [3]. He puts the win rate at about 70%, with most losses on cost [3]. The business development team is 25-30 people out of roughly 550 [3]. In Oman the company ranked first on technology but second on price, and the customer asked it to negotiate further [3]. So a tender win is part product, part price, part pre-selling, and it is never guaranteed.

The second route is partners. SoftTech is an Autodesk developer-network member and value-added reseller, and it earned ₹6.44 crore from Autodesk's channel in FY2017 [2]. It signed a sales partnership with CGI, a large government-technology integrator in the US and Canada, and with CDCi in Malaysia [9]. The CEO says its CivitSUSTAIN order from Mitsubishi Electric rides on controllers that Mitsubishi supplies to L&T for city water networks [3]. For Germany, management leans on the network of its investor Thomas Wolf, whose RIB group sold construction software there for thirty years [3]. The annual report describes the plan as relying on 'partner-led go-to-market models rather than on the direct establishment of large overseas sales organisations', a capital-light stance that also means SoftTech does not control the customer relationship [1].

web_blocks.takeaway: Almost every route ends at a government buyer; only the applicant-pays routes spare SoftTech a government invoice.

web_blocks.html: From award to cash the cycle has five steps. First, the contract. Second, requirements and rule codification, where SoftTech reads the authority's regulations and turns them into logic. Third, configuration, data migration and integration with GIS, payment gateways and other departments' systems. Fourth, user acceptance and go-live. Fifth, operations and maintenance, or pay-per-use billing. How long does it take? The Madhya Pradesh permit contract for 14 corporations ran from June 2013 to December 2018 [2]. At the 2024 AGM the then CFO, Kamal Agarwal, said the ₹287 crore order book would convert over about three years on average, while the CEO put the window at three to five years [9]. In FY2026 about 40% of the AAI order was recognised in the first year and the rest follows over roughly three years [3]. JNPA expects core functions by February 2027 and full operation by February 2028, about 17 months from award [12].

The order book needs care. It was ₹287 crore in September 2024 [9], ₹231.99 crore after FY2026 [1], and ₹302.35 crore at 6 November 2026 [10]. Strip out the ₹92.95 crore JNPA order and the November figure is about ₹209 crore, below September 2024 even though revenue has grown some 70% since FY2024 (my arithmetic on [9][10][12]). The pipeline of qualified bids was ₹436.23 crore in June and ₹625.57 crore in November; management says it converts at 'more than about 60%' [3][10]. The accounts offer a harder number: unsatisfied performance obligations of ₹114.64 crore at March 2026, up 40% from ₹82.01 crore, which is roughly half the stated order book; the filings do not reconcile the two measures [1].

Now billing. The accounts say 'the billing schedules agreed with customers include periodic performance based payments and / or milestone based progress payments', with invoices payable 'within contractually agreed credit period' [1]. Fixed-price work is recognised over time using an output measure (plans approved, transactions processed, software phase completed); licences are recognised on delivery; maintenance is spread evenly [1]. The gap between revenue recognised and invoices raised is parked on the balance sheet as a contract asset, or unbilled revenue. In FY2026 SoftTech recognised ₹74.11 crore of revenue on such contracts and billed ₹63.05 crore, so about ₹11 crore of earned revenue is still waiting to be invoiced [1]. The auditor made revenue recognition on fixed-price contracts a key audit matter because the choice of milestone and method needs judgement [1].

web_blocks.caption: Billing and cash-cycle facts, consolidated, March 2026 vs March 2025
rows: Both together as share of revenue
Debtor days in the data feed (trade receivables only)
Credit-loss charge in profit and loss
web_blocks.takeaway: Collections improved, but a fifth of billed-plus-unbilled balances is now provided for, and four-tenths of receivables are over a year old.

web_blocks.html: What the table shows is real improvement from a very stretched position. Trade receivables fell ₹9 crore while revenue grew 40%, and management cut DSO (days sales outstanding, the average days to collect) from 372 to 260, with a goal below 200 [3]. What it does not show is cure. The company provided ₹17.65 crore against ₹105.80 crore of gross receivables and unbilled revenue, 16.7% of the balance, and the charge to profit and loss rose from ₹2.79 crore to ₹12.49 crore [1]. The CFO says the cause is that governments hold back '1%, 2% of our invoice values' until later and that a new policy now reserves long dues; the CEO adds that retentions and deposits can take 'sometimes even seven years' to come back [3]. He is candid about the structure: 'government is also, I would say, a risk free business in a way. But the challenge is collecting at time' [3]. Receivables are pledged to banks as security for working-capital lines, and the auditor's CARO report records that quarterly returns filed with those banks did not agree with the books: ₹2.85 crore short in June 2025, ₹1.70 crore short in September, ₹12.35 crore higher in December and ₹15.95 crore short in March, which management attributes to returns being filed provisionally before closing adjustments [1].

The other cash drain is capitalised development. Under accounting rules a software company may treat engineering cost for a new product as an asset, not an expense, once the product is technically and commercially feasible, then write it off over its useful life. SoftTech paid ₹30.50 crore for intangible development in FY2026, 22.9% of revenue, and ₹34.47 crore in FY2025, 36.2% of revenue [1]. It amortised ₹20.44 crore in FY2026, with the CEO citing a three- to four-year life [1][3]. Intangible assets and those under development stand at ₹90.22 crore, 53% of total equity [1]. The auditor lists this as a key audit matter and tested payroll, vendor contracts and invoices on a sample basis [1]. Two readings are possible, and both are fair. One: this is investment in products that now earn transaction fees. Two: it is a way of moving operating cost from the profit statement to the balance sheet. Pay-per-use contracts make the second risk sharper, because SoftTech funds the customisation up front.

Now follow ₹100 of FY2026 revenue through the audited consolidated statements, one period throughout: profit and loss and cash flow both for the year to 31 March 2026. Of every ₹100, ₹14.45 pays for resold software, ₹24.83 pays staff, and ₹36.50 pays other expenses. Within those other expenses, ₹17.05 is outside technical consultants and ₹9.40 is the credit-loss provision. That leaves EBITDA (profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) of ₹24.22. Depreciation and amortisation take ₹17.18, interest ₹3.06, other income adds ₹2.74, and tax takes ₹2.71, leaving profit after tax of ₹4.01 [1].

web_blocks.caption: SoftTech Engineers, year ended 31 March 2026, consolidated audited statements, ₹ crore, scaled to ₹100 of revenue. Cost of goods is traded-software purchases less the change in stock; capex is property and equipment (₹2.07 crore) plus capitalised development (₹30.50 crore); tax is current plus deferred.
web_blocks.takeaway: About ₹24 of every ₹100 of revenue survives to EBITDA and about ₹24 reaches the operating cash-flow line, but capitalised development and equipment spending of ₹24.5 absorbs all of it, leaving free cash flow of about minus ₹1.

web_blocks.html: Read the cash half carefully. Operating cash flow was ₹31.26 crore, or ₹23.52 per ₹100 of revenue. It started from ₹46.13 crore of cash generated before working capital, but ₹12.98 crore of that is simply adding back the credit-loss provision, which is a non-cash charge, and then ₹10.46 crore went into working capital and ₹4.41 crore into tax [1]. Capex was ₹32.57 crore, ₹24.51 per ₹100, of which ₹22.95 is capitalised software and ₹1.56 equipment. Free cash flow was therefore about minus ₹1.31 crore, minus ₹0.98 per ₹100; the company's own standalone figure is minus ₹0.09 crore [1]. Take lease payments of ₹1.79 crore and interest paid of ₹3.44 crore as well and the stricter figure is minus ₹6.53 crore. In effect 98% of operating cash went into new software. The data feed shows free cash flow negative in each of the eight years FY2019 to FY2026, about minus ₹46 crore in total, against cumulative group profit near ₹34 crore (rounded data feed). The gap was financed by the IPO, preferential issues and borrowings: ₹31.74 crore of debt against ₹33.00 crore of cash and bank deposits at March 2026 [1].

Some unit economics are disclosed, and they point different ways. Revenue per employee was ₹22.8 lakh and employee cost per head ₹5.7 lakh across 582 staff, but ₹22.66 crore went on outside technical consultants, so the real delivery workforce is larger than the payroll [1]. Resold software earns about 13.6 paise per rupee [1]. The TDR exchange, if volume returns, is described as a 70-80% margin stream [3]. Pay-per-use brings cash as the permit is issued, and the CEO says it 'improves our cash flow positions' [3]. Add back the ₹12.49 crore provision and EBITDA would have been about 33.6% of revenue instead of 24.2%, which is the margin management points to; whether that provision proves temporary is the central cash question for FY2027 [1][3].

Follow one invoice from SoftTech's side. A project manager at SoftTech reaches a contract milestone: the permit workflow is configured for a state's 40 towns. She asks the authority's engineer to certify completion. The engineer takes a few weeks, and then the file goes to the accounts section, where an officer checks the sanction, the budget head and the tender terms. The bill is approved, sent to the treasury, and eventually paid, minus a retention of one or two per cent that stays with the department for years, sometimes up to seven [3]. Every stage of that walk is outside SoftTech's control, which is why the company's most valuable commercial innovation may be a boring one: ask the architect to pay at the moment of the permit.

If I were at the table with the CFO, Deepak Bang, I would ask four questions. How much of the ₹17.65 crore allowance relates to customers who are disputing the work, and how much to customers who are simply slow [1]? When is the allowance expected to reverse, and in which line will the reversal appear? Of the ₹30.50 crore capitalised last year, how much was salaries of SoftTech's own staff and how much was outside consultants [1]? And what is the free-cash-flow breakeven for the business if pay-per-use reaches half of sales?

Warren Buffett once warned that 'managers that always promise to make the numbers will at some point be tempted to make up the numbers'. That is not an accusation here: the audit opinion is unmodified, though the auditor's CARO report carries two exceptions, and the company discloses its judgements openly [1]. It is a reminder to read cash alongside profit. Profit after tax of ₹5.33 crore looks healthy beside revenue growth of 40%; operating cash of ₹31.26 crore looks healthy too; but cash after the software the company had to build was close to zero.

In plain language: SoftTech wins orders by bidding on government tenders and partnering with larger technology firms. After winning, it builds and configures software for months or years, and bills in stages. Between the work and the cash sit unbilled revenue, approvals, and often delays by the government. The company has been shortening that wait, and its new pay-per-use and exchange models are designed to cut it further. For FY2026, though, almost all the cash the business made was spent on building the next round of software [1][3].

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The product earns its margin when a city adopts the rule engine; it earns its cash only when the payer, usually a government office, releases the money. In FY2026 SoftTech closed the gap noticeably, with DSO down from 372 to 260 days, but 98% of operating cash flow still went into capitalised software. Keep the two clocks separate: orders tell you about demand, and the cash-flow statement tells you whether growth pays for itself.
